title: Emergence of Hexanematic Order in a Growing Confluent Cell Monolayer
authors: Hon Lin Too, Farisan Dary, Isaac Si Yuan Ling, Dustin Erhard Theofilusa, Duo Zhang, Haiyi Liang, Ee Hou Yong
abstract: Collective migration of epithelial layers underlies processes ranging from wound healing to cancer invasion. A defining yet challenging feature is the emergence of distinct cell morphologies within a single migrating confluent sheet, with larger, elongated cells at the active boundary and smaller, hexatically ordered cells in the bulk. Here, we develop a stochastic particle-Voronoi framework that captures this hexanematic organization without prescribing target geometries and distinct cell types. We show that boundary-driven collective motion generates an outward velocity gradient. This gradient, coupled to a density and velocity-dependent division rule, produces peripheral cells that are larger, more elongated, and more defect-prone, while bulk cells remain smaller, isotropic, and hexagonally packed. These results show how minimal, non-equilibrium mechanical interactions give rise to emergent, self-organized tissue-scale patterning during collective migration.
summary: This work models collective cell migration using a stochastic particle-Voronoi simulation. It demonstrates that simple mechanical interactions create an outward velocity gradient, which spontaneously organizes the monolayer into distinct regions: tightly packed, hexatically ordered bulk cells, and larger, more elongated peripheral cells. This highlights how complex tissue patterning can arise from minimal local physical rules.
main_problem: The study investigates how distinct cell morphologies (hexanematic vs. elongated) emerge spontaneously within a single, growing confluent epithelial monolayer during collective migration.
main_result: The authors show that minimal, non-equilibrium mechanical interactions generate an outward velocity gradient, which drives the spontaneous segregation into highly ordered bulk cells and more spread peripheral cells.
method: A stochastic particle–Voronoi framework is developed to simulate cell dynamics, incorporating coupled Stochastic Differential Equations (SDEs) for cell velocity and motility vectors.
model_or_system: The model simulates confluent cell monolayers using a Voronoi tessellation approach. Cell movement is governed by mechanical interactions derived from the particle positions, allowing for adaptive growth and division based on local density and area thresholds.
key_observables: Local mean cell area ($\langle A(x) angle$), hexatic order parameter ($|\gamma_6|$), topological defect density ($s$), and spatial velocity gradients.
important_parameters: Division radius ($R_d$), noise amplitude ($\sigma_i$) which is density-dependent, and the coupling constants within the SDEs.
main_assumptions: The emergence of pattern is attributed solely to minimal local mechanical rules, without pre-specifying cell types or target geometries; periodic boundary conditions are used along one axis.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate time-lapse images showing peripheral elongation versus bulk regularity, and spatial profiles demonstrating the inverse correlation between hexatic order (high in the bulk) and cell area (increasing toward the front).
paper_structure: The paper introduces the stochastic particle-Voronoi model, details the governing SDEs and boundary conditions, presents simulations showing morphological segregation and defect accumulation, and concludes by interpreting these findings as evidence for emergent tissue patterning driven by mechanical gradients.
why_interesting: While focused on biology, the underlying mathematical framework—modeling pattern formation, phase transitions (hexatic order), and non-equilibrium steady states using stochastic dynamics—is highly relevant to active matter physics studied in AMO and statistical mechanics.

(A) Time-lapse images of wound closure in a HeLa cell monolayer: peripheral cells are larger and elongated, while bulk cells are smaller and more regular. (B) Boxplot of the border speed measured across 11 independent experiments, with a mean value of 6.0µm/hr. (C) Particle distribution before Voronoi tessellation. Blue: real particles; grey: periodic copies. The alpha shape defines the boundary, which is offset outward to place ghost particles. (D) Illustration of particle dynamics. Cell velocity and motility vector are updated through interactions with Voronoi neighbors. (E) Simulation workflow.

(C and D) Histogram of cell polarity magnitude and (E and F) polar plot of cell polarity orientation, averaged over 10 independent simulations.
